messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]
Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 46-year-old Caucasian male, was admitted to the hospital due to a new onset headache, nausea, and vomiting. The patient had a history of pancreatic cancer with metastases to the liver and omentum, and had undergone treatment with chemotherapy. The patient was also previously hospitalized for a pulmonary embolism and small bowel obstruction.

Upon admission, the patient presented with dull, intractable headache, icteric eyes, decreased air entry, and decreased muscle strength. The patient reported hitting his head in the bathroom one week prior to admission and had a family history of colon cancer.

During hospitalization, the patient developed syncope and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Imaging studies revealed bihemispheric subdural hematomas and left hemispheric extra-axial metastatic lesions. The patient was started on levetiracetam and received cranial irradiation with right and lateral fields. The treatment significantly improved the patient's headache and nausea, and he did not experience any new seizures.

The patient tolerated radiotherapy well and did not require a treatment break. However, he died 2.5 months later at home. No autopsy was performed as per family request.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:

Ondansetron, metoclopramide, and dexamethasone
Levetiracetam
Cranial irradiation with right and lateral fields

Follow-up:

The patient passed away and there is no follow-up needed.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Allergies:

Not reported.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient passed away.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
1. The admission was chiefly for symptomatic intracranial (extra-axial, likely dural) metastases from pancreatic cancer, treated with cranial irradiation, dexamethasone and levetiracetam; the subdural haematomas and seizure were consequences.
2. Secondary malignant neoplasms fall in chapter C.
3. Metastases to the brain or meninges belong in category C79 (secondary malignant neoplasm of other sites).

CODE: C79
